children: Mafatlal Industries CFO highlights the need to improve capital turnover, reduce production delays and strengthen higher-value manufacturing to boost export performance

Turn over the label on a cotton T-shirt in an Indian store and, often, it reads “Made in Bangladesh” or “Made in Vietnam”. For a country with more cotton acreage than almost any other, one of the world’s largest spinning bases, and an estimated 45 million people employed directly in textiles and apparel, that small tag tells an uncomfortable story.

India has never lacked scale. In 2000, both Bangladesh and Vietnam trailed India in global apparel exports. Since then, Bangladesh and Vietnam have significantly strengthened their positions in global apparel exports, highlighting the gap between India’s manufacturing scale and its export performance. The sector still earns the country around USD 37 billion a year in exports, but it is not yet reaching the wardrobes of the world in the way our size suggests it should.

Observing the industry through the lens of capital, cash and returns, the next phase of Indian textile competitiveness will be decided less by how much we can produce and more by how efficiently each rupee in the chain is put to work.
Capacity Where Value Is Thinnest

Consider how value is created. A kilogram of raw cotton costing about Rs 170 can become two or three finished garments worth Rs 800 to Rs 1,000. Most of that multiplication, and most of the jobs, sit at the end of the chain, in cutting, stitching and finishing. Yet India’s depth is concentrated upstream, in spinning, where margins are thin and cyclical.

Strengthening capabilities in higher-value segments, alongside India’s established spinning capacity, presents an opportunity to capture greater value across the textile value chain. While China and Vietnam developed large, integrated manufacturing hubs, India’s garment sector continued to be characterised by smaller production units.

India’s textile manufacturing ecosystem presents opportunities to strengthen integration across labour-intensive industries through continued improvements in infrastructure, access to finance and supplier networks. Today, more than 80 per cent of Indian apparel units are micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and a single garment can travel from cotton grown in Gujarat to yarn spun in Tamil Nadu and fabric woven in Maharashtra before it is ever stitched.

From a finance perspective, the most underestimated cost in Indian textiles is not wages or power. It is time. Every handover in a fragmented chain adds freight, inventory, receivables and a few more days to the cash conversion cycle. A global brand placing a seasonal order cares about price but rewards reliability and speed. A supply chain that is cheap on paper but slow in practice loses the order. For manufacturers, reducing these delays can improve inventory turnover, lower working-capital requirements and free up capital for growth without necessarily adding new capacity.

The evolution of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) framework has been an important development for India’s textile industry, with the GST rationalisation effective from September 2025 reducing the rates on man-made fibres and yarns to 5 per cent. In a low-margin business, effective management of inventories and tax credits remains important to maintaining liquidity and supporting growth. Improving working-capital efficiency and accelerating capital turnover can help manufacturers strengthen competitiveness.
The Wrong Cost Curve

The world has also moved on from the fibre India knows best. Fast fashion, athleisure and activewear have pushed man-made fibres to around 70 per cent of global fibre consumption, while roughly 60 per cent of India’s yarn output is still cotton. India’s cotton yields are about half the global average, and domestic prices can swing by 18 per cent to 22 per cent in a year. For a finance team, that is input-cost risk capable of wiping out a season’s margin.

On labour, the average Indian garment worker earns around USD 200 a month, against about USD 120 in Bangladesh. India’s competitiveness cannot rest on wages alone. Sustained gains will depend on improving output per worker, increasing machine utilisation and generating higher output for every rupee of capital employed.
A Window That Will Not Stay Open

The global sourcing map is being redrawn. Restrictions on Xinjiang cotton have pushed buyers to diversify away from China, whose share of global apparel exports has fallen meaningfully over the past decade. Bangladesh faces energy and political strains, and its graduation from least developed country status will, after a transition period, end its duty-free access to the European Union.

This is a generational opportunity for India. Progress on a trade agreement with the European Union, more stable access to the United States, the seven PM MITRA parks being developed with an outlay of Rs 4,445 crore to bring spinning, weaving, processing and garmenting under one roof, and labour codes that ease the incentive to stay small all point the same way.

The World Bank’s recent work on the global jobs challenge reinforces the case: the economies that sustained employment booms did so on the back of sustained investment growth, and value-added manufacturing is among the sectors that absorb the most workers. Public capital expenditure has done the heavy lifting. Private investment now has to follow.
But buyers leaving one market will not default to India. They will go wherever the total cost of sourcing, meaning price, speed, compliance and reliability together, is lowest.

Right now, India needs capacity that earns its keep: integrated, fast, compliant and disciplined in how it uses capital. The World Bank put it well when it said that population sets the stage, but policy writes the script. For Indian textiles, policy has begun to set the stage. How the industry allocates its capital will write the script.
Smita Jhanwar
Guest Author The author is Chief Financial Officer at Mafatlal Industries Limited.
